title: Some historians say he beat Marconi to radio waves. He never patented it. November 23, 2026.
excerpt: Jagadish Chandra Bose's uncredited radio breakthrough, a national milestone of 3.76 crore rural women crossing a lakh rupees in income, and the entrepreneur whose solar dehydrators are stopping harvests from going to waste.
bodyHtml:
Some historians say he beat Marconi to radio waves. He never patented it

Jagadish Chandra Bose, the physicist and biologist who pioneered radio wave research, died on November 23, 1937, in Giridih, Bihar. Bose demonstrated wireless signal transmission using microwaves as early as 1895 and was among the first to use a semiconductor junction to detect radio waves - work that predates Guglielmo Marconi's famous demonstrations, though Bose never patented it. He also invented the crescograph, a device to measure how plants respond to stimuli, and founded the Bose Institute in Kolkata in 1917, often called Asia's first interdisciplinary research centre.

3.76 crore rural women just crossed a lakh rupees a year in household income

A 'Lakhpati Didi' is a rural woman whose household income crosses one lakh rupees a year. As of June 2026, 3.76 crore rural self-help group women have reached that status - part of a self-help group network that has grown to over 10 crore members across 94.4 lakh groups nationwide. The government's target is 6 crore Lakhpati Didis by March 2029, meaning this milestone is already past halfway there.

Farmers were losing a third of their harvest to spoilage. She built a machine to stop that

Nidhi Pant co-founded S4S Technologies, building low-cost, solar-powered dehydration units that let farmers and rural women process surplus produce into shelf-stable products instead of losing it to spoilage. The model has turned rural women into micro-entrepreneurs, with reported income increases of up to 15% for the smallholder farmers it works with. In 2026, Pant won the Social Entrepreneur of the Year India award from the Jubilant Bhartia and Schwab Foundations - S4S had already won the Earthshot Prize for the same work.

Three stories today, one thread: credit that didn't matter as much as the work itself, a number that only exists because millions of smaller numbers added up, and a machine built to save what almost didn't make it to market.

coverHeadlines: A 'Lakhpati Didi' is a rural woman whose household income crosses one lakh rupees a year. As of this year, that's no longer a rare story - it's 3.76 crore of them.
Some historians say he beat Marconi to radio waves. He never patented it.
Smallholder farmers across India lose huge amounts of produce to spoilage before it ever reaches a market. Nidhi Pant built a machine small enough to fix that on the farm itself.
